query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (~1 at.%) of hafnium to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its high‐temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a dense, self‐healing oxide scale that limits oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with a BCC structure (e.g., a Ti-V-Nb-Ta based composition) without hafnium addition.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ~1 atomic percent Hf into the alloy composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at approximately 800°C for extended annealing (e.g., up to 24 hours), where oxidation typically proceeds at a measurable rate.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer that is enriched in Hf (and possibly forms HfO2 components) acting as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Hafnium, known to act as an oxygen scavenger, is expected to reduce the effective diffusivity and solubility of oxygen in the alloy. This promotes rapid reformation and densification of the protective oxide scale, thereby reducing oxygen ingress and delaying deleterious internal oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should demonstrate a significantly lower mass gain (by roughly 20–30% compared to the untreated alloy) during oxidation at 800°C, along with improved integrity of the oxide scale (reduced cracking/spallation), indicating enhanced oxygen resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed to the same oxidation conditions, which would develop a less protective and more porous oxide scale with higher oxygen uptake.
generation.boundary: This improvement is predicted for oxidation conditions around 800°C in air; at significantly lower or higher temperatures or under different atmospheric compositions, the effect may differ or be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and the detailed microstructural characteristics of the Hf-enriched oxide scale are uncertain and may depend on interactions with other alloying elements and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of the baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti-V-Nb-Ta based) and another set with an added ~1 at.% Hf. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation at 800°C in air for 24 hours. Use consistent processing and sample preparation methods for both groups.
measurements: Mass gain measurement (thermogravimetric analysis) during and after exposure to quantify oxidation rate.
Characterization of oxide scale morphology and composition (using scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy).
Assessment of oxide scale thickness and integrity (using cross-sectional microscopy).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-containing samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least a 20–30% decrease) in oxidation mass gain and fail to form a denser, more adherent oxide scale compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The CALPHAD calculations indicate that oxygen can substantially affect the phase stability in Ti-V-Nb-Ta. In the absence of oxygen, equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta is predicted to exhibit a single-phase BCC structure, while trace levels of oxygen facilitate the formation of the α-Ti phase at the aging temperature, consistent with oxygen’s role as an α-stabilizer in Ti alloy (). As nitrogen is also an α-stabilizer in Ti alloys, it may play a similar role to oxygen in facilitating the formation of α-Ti phase in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta. Grain boundary α-Ti precipitates are observed to nucleate initially, followed by the formation of intragranular precipitates and the emergence of PFZs adjacent to the grain boundaries. The experimental characterization and equilibrium phase calculations lead to the inference that the formation of PFZ in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta system is the result of diffusion of Ti and major interstitials (O and N) to grain boundaries, with subsequent formation of nitrogen- and oxygen-rich α-Ti precipitates at the aging temperature. Oxide scales will form on any alloy that is exposed to a reactive environment at elevated temperature(s). Stable protective scales are desirable for alloys used in structural applications at high temperatures. A scale can be damaged during service, for example, scale cracking and spallation could occur during thermal cycling owing to differences in the values of coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) between scale and substrate. Thus, healing of the scale via the reformation and growth of the protective oxides is another important requirement []. Wagner’s model for the transition from internal to external oxidation of an active element, like for example Al in Nb, gives the critical solute concentration that must be exceeded so that the outward diffusive flux of the active element is rapid compared with the inward diffusive flux of oxygen atoms []. Important parameters that determine the critical concentration of the active element are the solubility and diffusivity of oxygen, which must be reduced, and the diffusivity of the active element that must be increased. The addition of 6 at.% Ge in Nb-22Ti-12Si destabilised the Nb3Si, promoted the formation of Nb5Si3, significantly refined the microstructure and improved the high-temperature strength and room temperature fracture toughness respectively by about 88 and 19%, compared with the alloy without Ge []. The fracture toughness (KC, 3–point bend) of as-cast and heat-treated Nb-Ti-Si-Cr-Hf-Ge solid solution and silicide based alloys and the indentation toughness of the solid solution, Laves, and silicide phases have been reported []. The fracture toughness was not significantly changed by heat treatment and was about 10 MPa·m1/2 for alloys with more than 50 vol % silicide and Laves phases while the toughness of the solid solution ranged from 22 to 32 MPa·m1/2.
